'''''Quercus laurifolia''''' ('''swamp laurel oak''', '''diamond-leaf oak''', '''water oak''', '''obtusa oak''', '''laurel oak''') is a medium-sized semi-evergreen [[oak]] in the [[List of Quercus species|red oak]] section ''Quercus'' sect. ''Lobatae''. It is native to the southeastern coastal plains and south-central [[United States]].

== Description ==
''Quercus laurifolia'' is a [[tree]] growing to {{convert|65|–|80|ft|m|abbr=off|sp=us|order=flip}} (rarely to {{convert|130|ft|m|abbr=on|order=flip|disp=or}}) tall, with a large, circular crown. The [[leaves]] are broad lanceolate, {{convert|1|-|5|in|cm|abbr=off|sp=us|order=flip}} long and {{Convert|1.3-4.4|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad, and unlobed (very rarely three-lobed) with an entire margin and a bristle tip; they typically fall just as the new leaves start to emerge in spring. The [[acorn]]s, borne in a shallow<ref name="jacqui" /> or deep<ref name="jacqui" /><ref name=alden1999>{{cite book|title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to the Southeastern United States|last1=Alden|first1=Peter|last2=Cassie|first2=Brian|last3=Kahl|first3=Jonathan D.W.|last4=Nelson|first4=Gil|last5=Oches|first5=Eric A.|last6=Zirlin|first6=Harry|last7=Zomlefer|first7=Wendy B.|year=1999|publisher=Alfred A. Knopf|isbn=978-0-679-44683-5|page=100}}</ref> cup, are hemispherical<ref name="jacqui" /> or oblong,<ref name="jacqui" /><ref name=alden1999/> {{Convert|8.5|-|16|mm|sp=us|frac=16}}<ref name="jacqui" /> but up to {{convert|1|in|cm|spell=in}}<ref name=alden1999/> long, green, maturing blackish-brown about 18 months after pollination. Acorn production is often heavy, enhancing the species' value for wildlife.<ref name="jacqui" /> [[File:Quercus laurifolia (24141313266).jpg|left|thumb|The leaves of swamp laurel oak are occasionally three-lobed, as seen above.]]The seedlings show embryo [[dormancy]] and [[germinate]] the following spring after fall ripening; germination is [[hypogeal germination|hypogeal]].
Swamp laurel oak grows rapidly and usually matures in about 50 years.

A similar evergreen oak that also grows in sandy soils is ''[[Quercus hemisphaerica]]'', the sand laurel oak.

== Taxonomy ==
The botanist C.J. Burke<ref>Burke, C. J. (1961). An evaluation of three hybrid-containing oak populations on the North Carolina Outer Banks. Journal of the Elisha Mitchell Scientific Society 78(l):18-21.</ref><ref>Burke, C. J. (1963). The hybrid nature of Quercus laurifolia. Journal of the Elisha Mitchell Scientific Society 79(2):159-163.</ref> suggested that swamp laurel oak is of [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] origin having been derived from [[willow oak]] (''Quercus phellos'') and [[water oak]] (''Quercus nigra''); it is not found outside the ranges of the two supposed parental species. This conclusion was based on an index from leaf-shape on seedlings grown from acorns. However, this theory has not achieved wide support, with current authors accepting ''Quercus laurifolia'' as a distinct species (e.g. [[Flora of North America]]).<ref name=jacqui>{{eFloras|1|233501055|Quercus laurifolia |first=Kevin C. |last=Nixon |volume=3}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Swamp laurel oak grows from coastal [[Virginia]] to central [[Florida]] and west to southeast [[Texas]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.plantmaps.com/nrm/quercus-laurifolia-laurel-oak-native-range-map.php |title=Interactive Distribution Map of ''Quercus laurifolia'' |access-date=2010-08-22 |archive-date=2014-07-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140728145326/http://www.plantmaps.com/nrm/quercus-laurifolia-laurel-oak-native-range-map.php }}</ref> There are reports of the species growing in [[Pennsylvania]] and [[New Jersey]], but these probably represent introductions.<ref>{{BONAP|genus=Quercus|species=laurifolia|date=2014}}</ref>

The species is found mostly on [[alluvial]] [[flood plain]]s, from sea level up to {{convert|150|m|ft|abbr=on|sp=us}} altitude. It will tolerate the wetter sites in association with other oak species but will not live with continuous or prolonged [[flood]]ing. It is most often found growing in sandy soil near [[river]]s and along the edges of [[swamp]]s if not too frequently flooded. Swamp laurel oak grows in the [[hammock (ecology)|hammocks]] of central Florida and on sand hills adjacent to swamps in west Florida. Swamp laurel oak grows best on [[ultisol]]s and [[inceptisol]]s.

The range has average annual temperatures from {{convert|16|to|21|C|F}}. It can withstand extreme lows ranging from {{convert|−1|to|−28|C|F}}. Extreme highs range from {{convert|38|to|43|C|F}}.

It needs between {{convert|1250|-|1500|mm|in|abbr=on}} of rainfall a year. From {{convert|500|-|1000|mm|in|abbr=on}} of this is received during the growing season from April to September.

The laurel oak is probably one of the most cold-hardy evergreen oaks. Trees growing in [[Cincinnati]] indicate the laurel oak may be hardy even further north than previously thought tolerating temperatures lower than {{convert|−29|C|F}} and surviving into zone 5. In Cincinnati trees have been observed staying green well into December.

== Ecology ==
Known hybrids with ''Quercus laurifolia'' as one parent are with ''Q. falcata'' (''Q × beaumontiana'' Sarg.), ''Q. incana'' (''Q. × atlantica'' Ashe), and ''Q. marilandica'' (''Q. × diversiloba'' Tharp ex A. Camus).

The tree is host to the general oak-feeding insects but has no serious insect problems. Several species of ''[[Curculio]]'' weevils infest the acorns.

Despite their bitter kernel, the acorns are eaten by [[deer]] (including [[white-tailed deer]]), [[squirrel]]s, [[bird]]s<ref name="jacqui" /> (including [[duck]]s, [[bobwhite quail]] and [[wild turkey]]s), [[raccoon]]s and small [[rodent]]s.

== Uses ==
It is grown and marketed mainly as [[pulpwood]]. It is commonly used as an [[ornamental tree]] in landscaping because of its fast growth and pleasing appearance; it is planted with little regard to soil type.
